newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia braces for grand final frenzy
newsitem.headline: Australia braces for grand final frenzy

text.p: Sports-mad Australia was bracing on Friday for its biggest weekend of the year with the annual rugby league and Australian Rules football grand finals, events which have triggered virtual sporting civil wars.
The action kicks off in Melbourne on Saturday with the Aussie Rules grand final between North Melbourne and the Sydney Swans.

North Melbourne represent the 100-year-old, uniquely Australian game's heartland in the southern state of Victoria, while the Swans are 15-year-old newcomers and the only team from Victoria's neighbours New South Wales.
Sunday sees the final match of a tumultuous year for the Australian Rugby League, with ageing heavyweights St George pitted against the heavily-favoured but widely disliked Manly.
St George, a traditional powerhouse in the 88-year history of the Australian Rugby League (ARL), reached the grand final after being rated 100-1 outsiders at the start of the season.

The old working-class club from Sydney's southern suburbs, is in the Guinness Book of World Records for its 11 consecutive titles in the 1950s and 60s -- it is the only team to have achieved the feat in any football code.
But St George was almost forced to merge with another inner city club early this year because of financial problems.
It then lost two coaches and several key players in the fallout of the bitter battle for control of the game between the ARL and media tycoon Rupert Murdoch's banned rebel Super League.
Manly, a rich club from Sydney's exclusive northern beaches, is the team much of Sydney loves to hate.

Manly's number one fan, author Tom Keneally, reportedly told incoming New South Wales state police commissioner, Englishman Peter Ryan, that he should support Manly in order to assimilate into Sydney culture.
Others warned Ryan his job trying to clean up corruption in the state force would be even more difficult with the massive plunge in popularity support of Manly would bring.
Politicians have been quick to jump on the sporting bandwagon, with the state premiers of New South Wales and Victoria indulging in a week of sniping over the match.
Victorians have accused their northern neighbours of trying to usurp their game while Sydney supporters say Victorians are using dirty tricks to avoid being beaten at their own game.
Australia Prime Minister John Howard, whose electorate is in Sydney, on Friday came out in support of St George and the Sydney Swans, who both wear red and white playing strips.
"I'm going for a red and white double...St George by four or five, Sydney by 10," Howard told business leaders at a lunch in Melbourne.
